## Simple explanation

Inverse kinematics (IK) asks: what joint positions should a robot use to put
its hand, gripper, or other endpoint at a desired location? It works backward
from a target pose to possible movements of the robot's joints.

## Technical explanation

For a robot with joint configuration $\mathbf{q}$ and forward-kinematics
function $f$, IK seeks a configuration such that $f(\mathbf{q})$ matches a
target pose. Solutions can be non-unique, nonexistent, or constrained by
joint limits, collisions, and motion requirements. Numerical solvers often
minimize position and orientation error iteratively.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

IK connects perception and planning to physical action. A robot can use it
to reach an object or position a sensor, while learning-based systems may
help predict poses or select targets. A valid mathematical solution must
still be checked for reachability, collisions, and safe execution.

## How it works

The system receives a target position and often an orientation. An IK solver
uses the robot's kinematic model to find joint values that produce a close
matching pose. It may use a closed-form solution for simple mechanisms or an
iterative numerical method for more complex ones; limits and collision checks
can constrain the search.

## Practical example

A robot arm is asked to place its gripper at a point above a table. The IK
solver returns one or more joint configurations that reach the target. A
planner can then choose a collision-free path to that configuration.

## Common misconceptions

- Inverse kinematics is not always a unique inverse; many joint configurations
  can produce the same endpoint pose.
- A target may be unreachable or may violate joint or collision constraints.
- Reaching the final pose does not guarantee that the path to it is safe.
